Clara Miller, who had been quietly tidying a stray stack of papers, suddenly gasped as she uncovered a small, metallic tool hidden beneath a loose rug near the doctor’s chair. It was a thin, blackened rod, smelling faintly of the same grease Thorne had seen on the desk. Dr. Aris quickly stepped forward to retrieve it, claiming it was a specialized probe from his medical kit that must have fallen out when he rushed to check Sterling’s pulse.

Thorne crouched down, his fingers brushing the rug near the victim's feet. He found a small, peculiar indentation in the wool, not from a shoe, but something metallic and circular. Julian noticed his gaze and began to tremble even more violently, his teeth chattering in the cold. Marcus Reed stepped closer, looming over the young man with an air of righteous indignation. "Check his pockets again, Detective. I saw him stuffing something away when we first broke in." Thorne complied, reaching into Julian’s jacket and pulling out a crumpled envelope. It was an ultimatum from a notorious London bookie, demanding payment of a debt that exceeded Julian's entire inheritance. The boy let out a choked sob, his defense crumbling, while Dr. Aris watched the scene with a cold, analytical interest, his gloved fingers still tightening around the handle of his black bag.

Thorne turned his attention back to the hearth, where a faint, bitter smell of burning paper lingered. He used a pair of tongs to pull a charred fragment from the embers, revealing the word "Disinherit" in Sterling’s elegant script. Julian’s head snapped up, his eyes wide with horror as he realized the depth of the hole he was in. Marcus Reed stepped closer, his boots crunching on the glass shards, and pointed out a dark, oily stain on Julian’s sleeve that matched the grease on the desk. "You were searching for the new will, weren't you?" Marcus demanded, his voice echoing in the library. Julian shook his head violently, but Dr. Aris cut in, noting that the boy's physical agitation was consistent with the adrenaline spike one would expect after a violent struggle. Aris then reached for his bag to offer Julian a sedative, but Thorne noticed the doctor's fingers were impeccably clean, unlike Julian’s grease-stained cuff.

Thorne moved his attention to the victim’s neck, noticing a faint, circular bruise that had been partially obscured by the collar of Sterling's shirt. He pointed it out to Dr. Aris, who leaned in for a closer look, his spectacles catching the firelight. "A pressure point," the doctor observed clinically, "it seems someone held the victim in place with considerable precision before delivering the fatal strike." Marcus Reed immediately pivoted back to Julian, his voice booming in the quiet room. "The boy has spent years watching you work, Aris. He probably picked up enough of your medical tricks to know exactly where to grab an old man to keep him quiet." Julian shook his head in a daze, his midnight blue sleeve brushing against the side of the desk, but Thorne’s eyes remained fixed on the black grease—now also visible on the underside of the silver letter opener's hilt—noting that Julian’s hands were stained only with blood.

Thorne moved toward the hearth, where the last of the logs was crumbling into gray ash. He noticed a small, charred scrap of paper fluttering near the grate and used a pair of tongs to retrieve it. It was a fragment of a legal document—specifically, the previous version of Arthur Sterling’s will, which had designated a significant sum to a local medical research foundation. Dr. Aris adjusted his glasses, his expression softening into one of professional regret as he mentioned that he was a board member of that very foundation. Marcus Reed scoffed, pointing at Julian again. "The boy must have tried to burn the old evidence of his exclusion to ensure no one questioned the sudden change in the ledger." Julian shook his head, staring at the soot on his own sleeve, which he hadn't noticed until that very moment, his face turning a deeper shade of panicked red.

Thorne stepped toward the dying embers of the fireplace, using the brass poker to shift the cooling logs. Tucked beneath a half-burnt oak limb was a singed envelope, which he carefully retrieved. Upon unfolding the charred paper, the detective revealed a desperate plea in Julian’s erratic scrawl, begging his uncle to pay off a local bookie before "things turned violent." Marcus Reed pointed a gloved finger at the document, his voice a low growl of triumph. "It’s a motive as old as time, Thorne. Greed and fear make for a bloody combination." Julian looked up, his eyes wide and bloodshot, but before he could speak, Dr. Aris reached out to adjust the victim’s collar, his movements smooth and practiced. The doctor noted the absence of any defensive wounds on Arthur’s hands, suggesting he never saw the blow coming—or that he trusted his killer completely.

Thorne moved back to the desk, his fingers tracing the smudge of black grease. "This isn’t ink," he murmured, rubbing the residue between his thumb and forefinger. Marcus Reed stepped closer, squinting at the mark. "It’s likely just soot from the fireplace, Thorne. The boy has been stumbling around this room in a panic; he probably touched the grate." Dr. Aris stepped forward, his eyes following the movement of Thorne’s hand. "It has a distinct viscosity, almost like machine lubricant," the doctor observed, his voice calm and professional. Julian, still slumped in the chair, looked up with hollow eyes, his voice barely a rasp as he claimed he had never even approached the desk until he saw the ledger. But Clara Miller pointed a trembling finger toward Julian’s shoes, where a similar dark streak was now visible on the side of his right leather boot, further cementing his presence at the scene of the crime.

Thorne walked to the heavy door and crouched down, examining the splinters where Marcus Reed had forced his way in. The wood was jagged and freshly broken, confirming Reed’s account of having to use his shoulder to gain entry. "It took some strength," Marcus grunted, rubbing his arm. "And Julian didn't make a sound from inside, did he, Clara?" The housekeeper nodded weakly, leaning against the wall for support. Thorne’s fingers brushed the floor near the frame, where a few tiny, black flakes of what looked like metal filings were scattered. Dr. Aris stepped over, his medical bag clicking as he moved, and peered down through his glasses. "The wear and tear on an old house," the doctor suggested smoothly, his voice devoid of emotion. Julian looked up, his face etched with terror, and screamed that someone had been hiding behind the curtains when he first entered, but the detective’s earlier inspection of the window area had found nothing but heavy, undisturbed velvet.

Thorne turned the blackened key over in his palm, his brow furrowed as he felt the lack of heat radiating from the metal. "If this was in the fire, it should be scalding," Thorne remarked, his voice barely a murmur over Julian’s soft whimpering. Marcus Reed stepped closer, his heavy boots thumping against the floorboards. "Perhaps the fire was lower when he threw it in, Detective. Don’t let the boy’s theatrics distract you from the obvious." Dr. Aris sighed, a sound of weary professional patience, and suggested that Julian might be suffering from a dissociative break brought on by the trauma of his own actions. The doctor’s hands, clad in thin surgical gloves, reached out to steady Julian, but the young man flinched away, staring at the doctor’s bag with a look of pure, unadulterated terror that seemed to transcend the situation at hand. Clara Miller watched from the doorway, her hands twisting her apron into tight knots, her eyes darting between the key and the doctor’s calm, steady hands.

"It is indeed curious," Thorne said, his voice dropping to a low rumble as he turned the blackened key over in his palm. Marcus Reed shifted his weight, the floorboards groaning beneath his heavy boots, and demanded to know why the boy hadn't been restrained yet. "He’s obviously guilty, Thorne. The sedative, the watch, the vault key—what more do you need? A written confession?" Julian, still slumped in the chair, looked up with hollow eyes, his voice barely a rasp as he claimed the key had been on the mantelpiece earlier that evening. Dr. Aris stepped back, his shadow stretching long and thin across the Persian rug, and suggested that perhaps the stress of the inheritance had finally pushed Julian over the edge. Clara Miller, meanwhile, had begun to clear away the shattered glass with a dustpan, her movements mechanical and her eyes fixed strictly on the floor, avoiding the dark pool of blood that continued to spread near the desk.

Thorne led the group toward the grand staircase, his hand firmly on Julian’s arm to prevent any desperate flight. They reached the master bedroom, where the heavy steel door of the wall vault stood agape, its contents vanished. Marcus Reed stormed inside, pointing at the empty velvet trays that had once held the Sterling family diamonds. "Empty! Every last stone gone!" Marcus roared, turning his fury back toward the trembling boy. "Where did you hide them, Julian? Under a floorboard? In the garden?" Julian could only shake his head in a state of near-catatonic shock, his eyes fixed on the vault’s intricate dial. Dr. Aris stepped closer, adjusting his spectacles as he examined the locking mechanism. He observed that there were no scratches on the dial, suggesting it had been opened by someone who either knew the combination or possessed the delicate tools of a professional. Clara Miller stood in the doorway, her hands tucked into her apron, her gaze lingering on the empty trays with a look that was more sorrowful than surprised.

Thorne stepped toward the window again, his fingers tracing the edge of the heavy velvet curtains where a faint, dark smudge of oil stained the fabric near the latch. Marcus Reed let out a short, triumphant laugh, pointing a thick finger at Julian’s trembling hands. "The boy’s been trying to grease the mechanism for weeks, Thorne! He’s been planning this ever since the old man threatened to cut him off." Julian’s protest was weak, his voice barely a whisper as he claimed he hadn't touched the window since the storm began. Dr. Aris stepped closer to the smudge, his spectacles catching the firelight as he remarked on how precisely the oil had been applied, a task that would require a remarkably steady hand. Clara Miller watched from the doorway, her knuckles white as she gripped her apron, her eyes darting between the detective and the doctor’s medical bag.

Marcus Reed didn't wait for Thorne to finish his thought about the key's temperature; he lunged toward Julian, grabbing the boy by the lapels of his midnight-blue jacket. "Where is the rest of it, Julian? Where is the money you stole from the vault?" Julian’s head snapped back as Marcus shook him, his cries for mercy echoing off the library walls. Clara Miller shrunk back into the shadows, her eyes darting toward the door as if she were looking for a way out. Dr. Aris remained by the desk, his expression a mask of clinical detachment as he watched the confrontation. "Violence won't bring Arthur back, Marcus," the doctor said softly, though his eyes never left the ledger. Thorne stepped between the two men, his gaze fixed on the black grease smudge on the desk. He noticed that the smudge was perfectly circular, as if a small, heavy object had been placed there recently and then removed.

Thorne signaled for the group to follow him to the master suite, where the heavy steel vault was hidden behind a portrait of Sterling’s late wife. Marcus Reed marched ahead, his shadow looming over the shivering Julian, who seemed barely able to stand. Clara Miller hovered at the rear, her eyes darting nervously toward the darkened corners of the hallway. When Thorne inserted the blackened key into the lock, the vault door swung open with a hollow click. The shelves were nearly bare, but a small stack of bonds was missing, replaced by a single, torn piece of a ledger page that appeared to be the missing half of the document downstairs. Marcus Reed let out a triumphant grunt, pointing to the torn edge. "He must have hidden the rest in his room, Thorne. The boy was systematic." Julian’s protest was a mere whimper, but Thorne’s attention was caught by the floor of the vault; a thin layer of white powder had settled there, and nestled within it was a small, round indentation, as if a heavy, circular object had recently been removed.

Thorne turned the key over in his palm, the soot staining his skin, yet the metal remained oddly chilled as if it had never truly tasted the fire's heat. "It wasn't in there long," Thorne remarked, his eyes shifting to Julian, whose face was a mask of sheer confusion. Marcus Reed stepped closer, his voice low and dangerous. "He probably panicked when he heard us coming and tossed it in, not realizing the fire was almost out. Typical of a boy who's never had to work for anything." Dr. Aris took the key from Thorne with a gloved hand, examining it under the lamplight. He noted that the key showed signs of recent filing, the edges sharp and bright beneath the layer of soot. Clara Miller whimpered from the corner, claiming she had seen the key on the master's nightstand just an hour before the murder, and Julian was the only one who had gone upstairs during that time. Julian's protests grew weaker, his spirit seemingly broken by the mountain of evidence stacking against him.

Thorne turned the blackened key over in his hand, noting that despite its soot-covered surface, it lacked the searing heat one would expect from a bed of coals. Marcus Reed stepped forward, his face a mask of righteous indignation. "He must have tossed it in just as we were breaking down the door, Thorne! He knew he couldn't hide it on his person once we caught him." Julian slumped further into his chair, his voice a broken rasp as he insisted he had never even seen the vault key before tonight. Dr. Aris walked over to the desk, his eyes scanning the ledger once more. He pointed out a small, smeared thumbprint in blood right next to the inheritance entry—a print that matched the size of Julian’s trembling thumb. Clara Miller let out a small, stifled sob, her hands twisting her apron into knots as she looked away from the boy’s condemned face. Thorne didn't speak; he merely looked at the smudge, then back at the "cool" key, his mind racing through the logistics of a room that had been sealed from the inside.

Thorne moved back to the mahogany desk, his gloved fingers tracing the edge where the black grease had been smeared. He pulled the ledger toward him, the heavy paper crinkling under his touch. The ink of the inheritance change was indeed fresh, but as he tilted the page toward the light, he noticed a curious lack of a blotter's mark, as if the writer had been in no hurry at all despite the supposed struggle. Marcus Reed leaned over his shoulder, his breath smelling faintly of peppermint and expensive scotch. "The boy was greedy, Thorne. He couldn't wait for the old man to die naturally." Julian let out a strangled cry of protest, but Dr. Aris interrupted, pointing out a small, circular bruise on the victim’s neck that had previously been hidden by his high collar. "An interesting mark," the doctor mused, his voice smooth and analytical, "almost as if someone had held him down with a firm, steady hand before the blade was used." All eyes turned to Julian’s trembling, slender hands, which looked far too weak for such a feat, yet the evidence continued to pile up against him like the drifting snow against the manor walls.

Thorne held the blackened key up to the light, noting how the soot came off in oily flakes on his fingertips. "If this key was in the fire," Thorne observed, "it hasn't been there long." Marcus Reed scoffed, stepping closer to Julian, who was trembling so violently that the chair beneath him rattled. "The boy probably tossed it in when he heard us coming to the door," Reed suggested, his voice low and dangerous. "He knew he couldn't hide the stolen bonds forever." Julian looked up, his eyes wide with a manic sort of fear, and shouted that he had seen Marcus Reed near the vault earlier that afternoon. The accusation hung in the air, but Reed merely pulled a heavy iron ring from his belt, showing a duplicate set of keys. "I’ve had my own access for years, boy. Why would I need to steal what I already manage?" Dr. Aris hummed thoughtfully, pointing out a small, fresh bruise on Julian’s neck that looked suspiciously like the mark of a struggle.

Thorne turned the blackened key over in his hand, noting that it was remarkably free of soot despite being pulled from the hearth. "This key wasn't in the fire for long," Thorne observed, casting a sharp look toward Julian. Marcus Reed sneered, stepping closer to the boy. "He must have tossed it in the moment he heard us at the door! A pathetic attempt to hide his greed." Julian shook his head, his voice a broken sob, insisting he hadn’t even known where the vault key was kept. Thorne then turned to Dr. Aris, who was carefully wiping his spectacles with a silk cloth. "You mentioned the blow was clean, Doctor. Almost surgical." Aris nodded, his expression remaining perfectly neutral. "Indeed. It requires a steady hand and a lack of hesitation—traits usually absent in a panicked youth." As Aris spoke, Thorne noticed a small, oily smudge on the doctor’s pristine white cuff, identical to the grease he had found on the mahogany desk and the door’s mechanism, though Marcus Reed was quick to interrupt, claiming he had seen Julian fiddling with the door’s hinges earlier that afternoon.

Thorne turned the key over in his hand, noting that it was remarkably clean of soot for something supposedly pulled from a bed of hot embers. Marcus Reed stepped closer, his shadow falling over the detective’s hand. "He probably tossed it in just as we were breaking down the door, Thorne. Trying to get rid of the evidence of his greed." Julian was huddled on the floor now, his voice a broken murmur of denials. Dr. Aris walked over to the desk and picked up the brandy decanter, sniffing the rim with a thoughtful frown. "The dosage of sedative in this glass was quite high, Detective. Enough to ensure the victim wouldn't—couldn't—resist a physical attack." Clara Miller looked toward the doctor, her eyes wide with a strange mix of fear and recognition, then quickly looked away when Aris met her gaze with a sharp, piercing stare. Thorne watched the interaction, then glanced back at the heavy library door, noting the absence of any scratch marks around the lock's interior face despite Julian’s supposed frantic movements.

Thorne led the group toward the master bedroom, the floorboards groaning under their collective weight. Behind a crooked oil painting, the wall safe stood ajar, its contents ransacked. Marcus Reed gestured wildly at the empty shelves, his voice booming in the narrow space. "He took the bearer bonds, Thorne! The boy knew exactly where the old man kept the emergency cash." Julian leaned against the mahogany bedpost, his face a mask of utter defeat as he insisted he had no knowledge of the safe's combination. Dr. Aris stepped forward, pulling a small magnifying glass from his pocket to inspect the dial. He noted aloud that there were no signs of a forced entry on the lock, suggesting the intruder either knew the code or had used a specialized tool to bypass it. As Aris spoke, his gloved fingers traced the dial with a strange familiarity, while Clara Miller watched from the doorway, her eyes fixed on the doctor's steady, unshakeable hands.

"It's silver-plated steel," Thorne remarked, his voice echoing in the hollow room as he held the key toward the light. "If it had been in the embers since the murder, it would have retained the heat far longer." Marcus Reed snorted, his face reddening with frustration. "Does it matter? The boy’s a thief and a murderer! Look at him, he can't even look us in the eye!" Julian Vane let out a pathetic moan, his body curled into a ball in the velvet chair. Clara Miller crossed her arms, her gaze fixed on the floor, while Dr. Aris adjusted the cuff of his own pristine shirt. The doctor pointed out that the sedative in the brandy would have taken at least ten minutes to render Arthur Sterling unconscious, a window of time that Julian claimed he spent outside the room. Marcus Reed stepped forward again, his heavy boots crushing a small piece of charcoal that had fallen from the hearth, his presence increasingly suffocating in the small library.

Thorne walked to the heavy wall safe behind a portrait of the Sterling family. He tried the blackened key he'd found in the fire, but it wouldn't even turn in the lock. Marcus Reed stepped forward, producing a ring of keys from his own pocket. "That's because that's not the safe key, Thorne. That's the key to the medicine cabinet in the guest wing," Marcus said, casting a sharp, knowing look at Julian. The young man’s eyes widened, his face becoming a mask of pure terror as he realized the implication. "I... I didn't mean to..." Julian started, but the words died in his throat as Marcus swung the safe door open, revealing it to be completely empty. "He’s cleaned it out, Thorne! The bonds, the cash—everything is gone." Julian collapsed further into his chair, the weight of the mounting evidence crushing the last of his resistance, while Dr. Aris looked on with a strange, almost pitying sigh.

Thorne held the blackened key up to the light, noting that the intricate warding was unusual for a simple vault. Marcus Reed shifted his weight, his leather boots creaking on the hardwood as he stepped closer to inspect the find. "That's definitely Arthur's key," Reed insisted, his voice booming in the quiet library. "Julian must have tried to hide it after he couldn't get the safe open." Thorne didn't respond immediately; instead, he walked over to the desk and compared the grease smudge to the residue on the key. It was a perfect match—a thick, industrial lubricant. He looked at Dr. Aris, who was currently adjusting the strap on his medical bag with gloved hands. The doctor met his gaze with a steady, clinical look, noting that such grease was often used for heavy machinery, or perhaps the internal mechanisms of high-end, complex locks that required constant maintenance to remain silent. Julian, still trembling, looked at the key with genuine confusion, claiming he had never seen it before in his life.

Thorne turned the soot-stained key over in his palm, noting that while the surface was blackened, the metal beneath was oddly free of the heat-induced pitting one would expect from a coal fire. Marcus Reed scoffed, stepping closer to Julian, who was now curled into a ball on the floor. "He probably threw it in the ashes just as we were breaking down the door, Detective. A last-ditch effort to hide his greed." Dr. Aris nodded in agreement, his gloved fingers adjusting the lapel of his immaculate coat. He pointed out that the victim's body was cooling at an accelerated rate, suggesting the murder had occurred shortly before Julian’s supposed discovery of the body. Julian looked up, his eyes bloodshot, and stammered that the room had been freezing since he arrived, but Clara Miller whispered that she had stoked the fire herself only an hour prior.

Thorne examined the heavy brass handle of the library door, then looked back at the smudge of black grease on the desk. Marcus Reed shifted uncomfortably, his large frame casting a shadow that seemed to swallow the small room. "I told you, I had to throw my whole weight against that door to get in," Marcus barked, his voice echoing off the high ceiling. Thorne reached out and took Marcus’s hand, turning it over to reveal a fresh, jagged scrape across the knuckles. "A souvenir from the door?" Thorne asked quietly. Marcus nodded, but Julian, emboldened by the momentary shift in focus, cried out that the door hadn't been stuck when he arrived. Dr. Aris stepped between them, his voice a calm, low drone as he suggested that the adrenaline of the moment might be clouding everyone's memory, though his eyes remained fixed on the "cool" vault key Thorne still held.

Thorne turned the soot-stained key over in his palm, noting how the black residue came off easily on his skin, revealing a surface that hadn't even begun to blister from the heat. He moved back to the ledger, and under the lamp's glow, he saw a faint, oily smudge near the binding—a match for the black grease on the desk’s edge. Marcus Reed stepped closer, his shadow stretching across the mahogany. "The boy is a thief and a murderer, Thorne. Let's not waste time over a dusty book. He’s already confessed to being in the room." Julian looked up, his eyes bloodshot. "I only said I was here after he was dead!" Dr. Aris adjusted his medical bag, his leather gloves creaking as he tightened his grip. The doctor calmly suggested that Julian’s erratic behavior was a classic symptom of the sedative's side effects, pointing out the boy’s twitching hands as further proof of his guilt. Thorne’s gaze shifted to the doctor’s pristine gloves, then back to the smudge on the desk.

Thorne walked toward the heavy safe hidden behind a portrait of the Sterling matriarch, the soot-covered key fitting perfectly into the lock. As the heavy door swung open, it revealed empty velvet-lined compartments where the family jewels and emergency cash were supposed to be kept. Marcus Reed let out a low, menacing growl, his eyes fixed on Julian’s shaking frame. "He’s already cleared it out! Check his coat, Thorne!" In a frantic bid to prove his innocence, Julian turned his pockets inside out, but as he yanked at the fabric, a hidden seam in his midnight-blue jacket tore open, spilling a thick stack of high-denomination banknotes onto the rug. The silence that followed was suffocating, broken only by Dr. Aris, who leaned forward to inspect the cash, noting that the bills were crisp and uncirculated, exactly the kind Sterling was known to keep for private transactions.

Thorne moved to the wall safe hidden behind the portrait of the family patriarch, the heavy silver key fitting perfectly into the lock. As the door swung open with a well-oiled whisper, Marcus Reed let out a triumphant grunt. "Empty! The boy must have cleared it out before he panicked and stabbed the old man." Julian buried his face in his hands, his muffled protests lost in the tension of the room. Thorne reached inside the velvet-lined safe, his fingers brushing against a small, discarded piece of paper—a receipt for a high-stakes gambling debt, dated only two days ago and signed by Julian Vane. Dr. Aris stepped forward, his eyes sharp behind his spectacles as he examined the empty interior. "It seems the financial pressure was even greater than we imagined," the doctor observed, his gaze drifting toward the black smudge on the desk again. Clara Miller stood by the door, her fingers twisting her apron so tightly that her knuckles were as white as the snow outside.

Thorne ignored Marcus’s outbursts and walked back to the fireplace, kneeling to retrieve the silver key again. He held it close to his face, sniffing the metal; it didn't smell of woodsmoke or ash, but of a faint, industrial lubricant. "A curious thing," Thorne muttered, "for a key supposedly tossed into a roaring fire to remain so cold and smell so... fresh." Marcus Reed folded his arms, his face a mask of annoyance. "Maybe the fire wasn't hot enough yet, or Julian just threw it in before you walked in." Julian shook his head, his voice a broken whisper. "I never saw that key. I didn't even know where he kept it." Dr. Aris stood by the desk, his hand resting near the black smudge. He pointed out that the lock on the safe seemed to have been recently oiled, a task usually reserved for the housekeeper. Clara Miller’s face went pale, and she stammered that she hadn't touched the safe in months, her eyes darting nervously toward the doctor's heavy medical bag.

Thorne turned his attention back to Dr. Aris, asking for a more precise estimate of the time of death. Aris knelt once more, his movements fluid and efficient as he checked for rigor and the cooling of the skin. "Forty-five minutes, Detective. Certainly no more than an hour," Aris stated, his voice clipping the words with professional certainty. This coincided perfectly with the time Clara had heard Julian arguing with his uncle. Marcus Reed leaned against the desk, his arms crossed, a dark smirk playing on his lips as he watched Julian’s spirit break. Thorne, however, was looking at the doctor’s medical bag again, noticing a set of surgical forceps peeking out from a side pocket—the tips of the metal were strangely bright, reflecting the firelight, while a small, dark smudge of grease sat just beneath the silver hinge of the tool.

Thorne turned the charred key over in his hand, his thumb brushing against a small, waxy residue on its edge. "The fire was hot enough to melt lead, yet this key is barely warm," he mused, looking toward Julian. Marcus Reed stepped forward, his eyes narrowed with impatience. "The boy probably just threw it in when he heard us coming, and it didn't have time to heat up! It’s another desperate attempt to hide his tracks." Julian shook his head, his face a mask of confusion and grief. "I didn't even know where the vault key was kept," he choked out. Dr. Aris moved closer to the desk, his gloved hand reaching out to touch the ledger’s spine. He pointed out a faint, oily fingerprint near the inheritance entry—a print that looked significantly larger than Julian’s slender fingers. Clara Miller gasped, her hand flying to her mouth as she looked from the desk to Marcus Reed’s heavy, calloused hands.

"I didn't put that there!" Julian cried, his voice hitting a shrill, hysterical note that echoed in the high-ceilinged library. Thorne didn't answer immediately, instead turning his attention to the floor directly beneath the wall safe. A few more of those tiny, black flakes were scattered there, identical to the ones he had found near the door’s broken frame. Marcus Reed stepped toward Julian, his face a mask of righteous fury as he towered over the boy. "You stole the key, you emptied the safe, and you killed him when he caught you. It's over, Julian. There’s nowhere left to run." Dr. Aris moved closer to the desk, his gloved fingers tracing the mahogany edge where the black smudge lay. He adjusted the heavy strap of his medical bag on his shoulder, the leather creaking softly in the sudden silence. Thorne watched the doctor's hands—noting the surgeon's precision in every movement—and then looked back at the trembling, clumsy boy who could barely hold a handkerchief without dropping it. Clara Miller let out a small, stifled sob, her eyes fixed on the empty safe as if she were seeing a ghost.

Thorne pulled a clean white handkerchief from his own pocket and carefully wiped the smudge of black grease from the edge of the mahogany desk. He rubbed the substance between his thumb and forefinger, finding it slick and oddly metallic; it wasn't grease at all, but finely powdered graphite, often used to lubricate high-precision mechanisms. Marcus Reed scoffed, dismissing the find as a triviality from the library’s clockwork, but Dr. Aris adjusted his glasses and leaned in, his interest piqued. "An odd place for lubricant, wouldn’t you say, Detective?" the doctor remarked, his voice smooth and steady. Julian Vane, still huddled in his chair, looked up with a flicker of hope in his tear-streaked eyes, while Clara Miller quietly began to collect the tea service she had left earlier, her movements stiff and mechanical. Thorne’s gaze shifted from the graphite to the heavy brass lock on the door, then back to the doctor’s impeccably clean medical bag.

Thorne turned his attention back to the mahogany desk, where the black smudge remained a silent enigma. He leaned down, sniffing the mark, and detected the faint, acrid scent of industrial lubricant, the kind used for delicate machinery or precision instruments. Marcus Reed scoffed, suggesting Julian had used it to grease the hinges of the door to sneak in undetected. "The boy's always been handy with tools, probably inherited it from his father's side," Reed added, his eyes narrowing. Julian looked down at his own trembling hands, which were indeed stained with a dark, oily substance that matched the mark on the desk. Dr. Aris stepped closer, his gloved fingers hovering just inches from Julian's skin, and noted that the substance appeared to be graphite, a common lubricant for high-end locks and medical equipment. Clara Miller let out a soft gasp, her eyes darting toward the heavy medical bag Aris held so tightly, but the doctor’s expression remained as cold and professional as the winter air.

Thorne returned to the mahogany desk, his magnifying glass catching the guttering candlelight as he examined the black smudge. "Graphite," he noted, his voice low. "Commonly used as a lubricant for intricate mechanisms or high-security locks." Marcus Reed pointed a thick finger at Julian, who was trembling uncontrollably. "He always was a tinkerer, Thorne. Probably spent half the night trying to bypass the safe before the old man walked in on him." Dr. Aris stepped closer, his gloved hands clasped behind his back. He suggested that the white powder found under the victim's fingernails might be residue from the struggle, perhaps scraped from the stone of the hearth as Arthur fought for his life. Clara Miller, however, didn't look at the hearth; her eyes were fixed on the doctor’s medical bag, which sat undisturbed near the desk, its leather surface gleaming under the library's dim lamps.

Thorne reached into the victim’s breast pocket, his gloved fingers extracting a folded piece of stationery. It was a letter, penned in Arthur Sterling’s shaky but elegant script, addressed to his lawyer. The letter expressed Arthur’s profound disappointment in Julian’s recent behavior and his intention to disinherit the boy entirely by the following morning. Marcus Reed leaned in, his eyes gleaming. "There’s your motive, plain as day. The boy killed him to stop that letter from being sent." Julian’s head snapped up, his eyes wild. "I didn't know! He never told me!" Dr. Aris adjusted his medical bag, the leather creaking in the silence. The doctor remarked that the ink on the letter was dry, suggesting it had been written hours before the murder, yet it remained in the victim's pocket. Clara Miller let out a soft, stifled sob, her gaze fixed on the floor, while Thorne noticed a tiny, almost invisible speck of that same black grease on the edge of the letter's envelope.

Thorne smoothed out the debt receipt, noting the jagged signature that matched Julian’s shaky hand. "This was quite the motive, wouldn't you say, Mr. Reed?" Marcus nodded, his arms still crossed tightly. "The boy was drowning. He needed the money now, not whenever Arthur decided to kick the bucket." Dr. Aris stepped closer to the desk, his gloved fingers hovering just inches over the black grease mark. He pointed out that the smudge had a curious, circular pattern, almost as if something had been rotated against the wood with great force. Julian looked up, his eyes bloodshot. "I didn't do it! I came in because I heard him fall! I saw the shadow behind the curtain, and then the door slammed! I didn't lock it!" Clara Miller let out a small, stifled sob, her eyes fixed on the floorboards where the black metal filings lay scattered like dark dust.

Thorne walked back to the desk, his eyes lingering on the black smudge that marred the polished mahogany. He pulled a magnifying glass from his coat and peered at the mark, which looked less like a simple stain and more like a precise, mechanical imprint. "Mr. Reed, you mentioned you had to force the door," Thorne said, not looking up. Marcus nodded curtly, his jaw set in a hard line. "I did. The boy had it bolted from the inside. Ask Clara, she saw me throw my weight against it." The housekeeper nodded, her voice barely audible as she confirmed the sound of splintering wood. Dr. Aris stepped closer, his gloved hand resting lightly on the edge of the desk, dangerously close to the smudge. "A tragic necessity," Aris remarked, "though it's a pity the lock was so resilient. It delayed us long enough for the life to drain out of poor Arthur." Julian let out a low moan, his head sinking back into his hands as the weight of the accusations seemed to physically crush him.

Thorne turned back to Dr. Aris, whose calm demeanor stood in stark contrast to Julian’s hysterical state. "Doctor, given the temperature of the room, what is your estimate for the time of death?" Aris stepped closer to the body, his gloved fingers hovering just above the wound without touching it. "I would say roughly twenty to thirty minutes ago, Detective. The blood is still relatively fresh, which aligns perfectly with when the household heard the disturbance." Marcus Reed leaned against the bookshelves, his eyes cold. "And conveniently, Julian was seen entering the library just five minutes before the scream." Julian shook his head, his voice a broken whisper, claiming he had been outside in the gardens to clear his head before his uncle summoned him. Thorne’s gaze shifted from Julian’s wet boots to the doctor’s medical bag, noting a faint, rhythmic clicking sound emanating from within the leather casing that Aris quickly silenced by shifting his stance.

Thorne reached into the pocket of the victim's dressing gown and pulled out a small, crumpled note. It was a frantic plea for money, written in Julian’s erratic scrawl, threatening "dire consequences" if the funds weren't delivered by midnight. Marcus Reed snatched the note, his face contorting with rage. "This is a confession in all but name! He killed him for the money, just as I said." Julian collapsed onto the floor, his head in his hands, unable to even speak through his tears. Dr. Aris stepped over the boy’s trembling form to offer Thorne a magnifying glass from his bag, his movements fluid and precise. "The ink is fresh," Aris noted, his voice smooth and devoid of any warmth. "It matches the pen on the desk perfectly." Thorne took the glass, but instead of looking at the note, he glanced at the doctor’s leather medical bag, which was sitting on the rug near a faint, oily stain.

Thorne turned away from the safe, his boots clicking on the hardwood floor as he approached Marcus Reed. "Mr. Reed, you were the one who forced the door, were you not?" Marcus nodded, his chest puffed out with a sense of righteous duty. Thorne reached out and took Marcus's hand, inspecting the sleeve of his heavy wool coat. There, near the cuff, was a faint, oily smudge, nearly identical to the one on the mahogany desk. Marcus pulled his hand away with a growl, claiming he must have picked it up when he leaned against the desk to check for a pulse. However, the detective’s attention was quickly pulled back to Julian when a heavy, ornate ring fell from the boy’s pocket and clattered across the floor. It was Sterling’s signet ring, the very one he used to seal his private correspondence. Julian scrambled to grab it, but Dr. Aris stepped on the boy’s hand, his expression one of cold, professional disdain as he looked at the clear evidence of theft.

Thorne ignored the tension and walked back to the heavy library door, his eyes tracing the line of the frame. Marcus Reed shifted his weight, his large frame casting a long shadow across the room. "Is there something about the door that troubles you, Thorne? It was locked from the inside—Julian’s cage." Thorne leaned in close to the brass strike plate, where the bolt had supposedly been slammed home. "It’s the lubricant," Thorne remarked softly, pulling a magnifying glass from his pocket. "A fresh application of graphite, used to ensure a mechanism moves without resistance." Dr. Aris stepped forward, his eyes following the detective’s hand. "In an old house like this, maintenance is constant, isn't it, Mrs. Miller?" Clara nodded quickly, her gaze fixed on the floor. Thorne noted that while the hinges were dry, the area around the bolt hole was slick with the black grease, a detail that didn't quite match Marcus Reed’s claim of having to use brute force to break in.

Thorne reached down and picked up a pair of discarded leather gloves from beneath the heavy mahogany desk, their palms blackened with grease and their fingertips stained a deep, rust-colored red. Marcus Reed let out a sharp, accusatory whistle. "There’s your murder weapon’s companion, Thorne. Julian spends half his life in the carriage house tinkering with those infernal engines. No wonder there's grease on the ledger." Julian stared at the gloves as if they were venomous serpents, his voice cracking as he insisted he hadn't seen them since Tuesday. Dr. Aris moved closer, peering through his spectacles at the dark smudges. "Interesting," the doctor noted softly. "The grease is remarkably fresh, yet Julian’s hands, though blood-flecked, seem quite free of any such industrial grime." Marcus's face hardened, and he dismissed the observation, claiming the boy must have used the handkerchief to wipe his hands before Thorne arrived.

Thorne walked back to the heavy oak door, his fingers tracing the edge of the frame where the black flakes had been found. Marcus Reed crossed his arms, his face flushed with a mixture of anger and impatience. "The boy had every reason to lock himself in, Thorne. He was cornered, his debts were piling up, and he knew his uncle was about to disinherit him." Julian looked up through his tears, his voice barely a rasp as he claimed the door had been bolted from the outside. Dr. Aris adjusted his medical bag, the leather creaking in the silence, and noted that such a feat would be physically impossible given the door's construction. Thorne, however, was looking at the small, discarded matchbox Clara had dropped earlier; he picked it up and found a tiny, bent piece of copper wire tucked inside the tray, a tool often used by those who know how to manipulate a bolt from the wrong side of a door. Julian’s eyes widened, but Marcus quickly pointed out that the wire was the exact gauge used in the clockwork of Julian’s own collection of mechanical trinkets, further tightening the noose around the young man’s neck.

Thorne moved back to the desk, his eyes lingering on the black smudge he had noticed earlier. He pulled a magnifying glass from his pocket and leaned in, his breath hitching slightly as he realized the smudge wasn't ink, but a heavy, industrial lubricant. Marcus Reed scoffed, his hands still deep in his pockets as he paced the length of the rug. "The boy probably got it on him when he was messing with the safe or the door, Thorne. He’s clearly desperate and clumsy." Julian sobbed, his head in his hands, but Dr. Aris walked over to the desk, his gaze following Thorne’s. The doctor pointed to a faint, corresponding mark on the edge of the ledger’s cover, a detail that Marcus had overlooked in his haste to condemn the boy. Clara Miller stood by the window, her breath fogging the glass as she whispered that she had seen Mr. Reed near the library earlier that afternoon, though he had claimed to be in the billiard room.

Thorne crouched by the desk once more, his fingers tracing the edge of the mahogany where the black grease smudge remained. He looked up at Julian, who was still trembling in the armchair. "Tell me about the lock, Julian. Did you use a key, or did you find another way in?" Julian shook his head, his eyes wide with terror, but Marcus Reed stepped forward and pulled a small, thin metal rod from the boy's coat pocket—a surgical probe, its tip stained with the same black grease that marked the desk. "He must have stolen it from the doctor’s bag!" Marcus shouted, his voice echoing in the library. Dr. Aris checked his bag, his face tightening as he confirmed the tool was indeed missing. Julian’s protests were drowned out by the weight of the evidence, as the probe matched the metal filings Thorne had found near the door.

Thorne turned his attention back to Julian, who was now clutching his stomach as if physically ill. "The receipt in the safe is for an immense sum, Julian. More than the inheritance would even cover." Marcus Reed stepped forward, looming over the boy. "He’s been stealing from the estate for months, Thorne. I found discrepancies in the books last week, and I told Arthur." Julian looked up, his eyes wild with a new kind of fear. "That’s a lie! You were the one who suggested the investments!" Dr. Aris moved to Julian’s side, ostensibly to check his pulse, but Thorne noticed the doctor’s sleeve brush against the desk, near the mysterious black smudge. As Aris withdrew his hand, his fingers seemed to linger for a fraction of a second on the edge of the ledger. Clara Miller let out a small cry, pointing to Julian's boots, where a stray, silver-tipped feather from the victim's writing quill had stuck to the heel.

Thorne moved back to the desk, his gloved finger tracing the black smudge once more. It was thick, like industrial lubricant, an oddity in a room filled with fine leather and polished wood. Marcus Reed followed him, his heavy boots thudding on the rug. "The boy's a mechanic in his spare time, isn't he? Always tinkering with those blasted motorcars. That grease probably came right off his hands before he put on those fancy gloves," Reed asserted, gesturing toward Julian’s discarded evening jacket. Julian looked up, his eyes wide and bloodshot, and stammered that he hadn’t touched a car in weeks since his uncle had forbidden the hobby. Dr. Aris leaned against the bookshelf, his medical bag still clutched in his hand, and pointed out that the grease seemed to have a metallic sheen, much like the shavings Thorne had found near the door. Clara Miller turned away, her face hidden in the shadows, as she began to gather the tea service with trembling hands.

Thorne carefully replaced the key in the safe and turned back to the room, his gaze lingering on the doctor’s bag before settling on Julian. "Mr. Vane, your uncle mentioned in his correspondence that you had once studied medicine at the university." Marcus Reed’s eyes lit up with a predatory gleam, his finger stabbing the air toward Julian. "He was a failure! Dropped out after two terms because he spent all his tuition on horses and cards!" Julian slumped even further into his chair, his voice barely a whisper as he admitted his brief medical background. Dr. Aris adjusted his spectacles, noting with a clinical coldness that the angle of the letter opener’s strike indeed required a rudimentary knowledge of the thoracic cavity—a skill a first-year student would certainly possess. Clara Miller let out a small, stifled sob, her eyes fixed on the empty brandy decanter, while Thorne moved to the desk once more to examine the black smudge that seemed to be spreading under the heat of the nearby lamps.

Thorne moved to the fireplace and poked at the grate once more, this time retrieving a small, blackened fragment of paper from the cooling ashes. It was a portion of a medical certificate, the names and dates charred away but the official seal still faintly visible. Marcus Reed’s eyes widened as he saw it. "He was trying to destroy his medical records! Or maybe something even more incriminating!" Julian’s face was a mask of sheer panic, his eyes darting toward the door as if he were looking for an exit that didn't exist. Dr. Aris leaned in, his expression unreadable, and observed that the seal was from a university that Julian had never attended. Clara Miller’s hands trembled so much that the tea tray she was holding clattered against the table, while Thorne turned back to the room, his eyes fixed on the black smudge on the desk that was now starting to look more like a fingerprint than a mere stain.Beneath the desk, Thorne noticed a single, pristine white button, its surface gleaming in the firelight. He picked it up with a handkerchief, noting its high-quality ivory and the way it seemed to have been torn from its thread. Julian’s midnight blue jacket was missing no buttons, nor was Marcus Reed’s charcoal wool coat. Thorne’s gaze drifted toward Clara Miller, who was now clutching her apron so tightly that she seemed to be trying to hide her own collar. Dr. Aris stepped closer, his medical bag clicking as he moved, and commented that the button looked remarkably similar to those on a professional lab coat—a detail that caused Marcus Reed to let out a short, sharp laugh. "Or perhaps a surgeon’s gown?" Marcus suggested, his voice dripping with suspicion as he looked at the boy once more. Julian looked down at his own buttons, his face a picture of bewilderment.

Thorne walked to the heavy door once more, this time focusing on the handle itself. The brass was cold and smooth, but he noticed a faint, oily residue on the inside of the latch. Marcus Reed watched his every move, his expression growing more frustrated as the detective continued to probe. "What are you doing, Thorne? The boy is clearly guilty. We have the motive, the weapon, and he was the one in the room!" Dr. Aris stepped forward, his eyes narrowing as he watched the detective’s hands. Thorne turned the knob slowly, then turned back to the room, his voice steady. "The key we found in the fireplace was to the safe, not the door. How was the door locked from the inside, and why did it have to be shoulder-butted open?" Julian sobbed, his head buried in his hands, his muffled voice a desperate plea of innocence while Clara Miller’s hands continued their relentless twisting. Thorne’s gaze settled on the heavy velvet curtains, noting how they hung slightly askew, as if something—or someone—had been hidden behind them during the initial chaos. 
"Indeed, the question is not who could have committed the murder, but who had the opportunity and the skill," Thorne said, his eyes scanning the faces of the four suspects. Dr. Aris’s fingers tapped rhythmically on his medical bag, his eyes tracking Thorne’s every move with a clinical curiosity while Marcus Reed’s shadow loomed large against the bookshelves. Clara Miller’s eyes darted toward the empty brandy decanter as if it held the answer, and Julian’s tears continued to flow, his voice a hoarse croak. Thorne’s gaze finally settled on the black smudge on the desk, his expression unreadable as he prepared to deliver his final revelation. 
"The key in the fireplace was not the only thing hidden in this room," Thorne said, his voice echoing in the quiet of the library. "There is one more piece of evidence that has been overlooked." 
Thorne moved to the fireplace and used the iron rod to probe the ashes once more. Among the dying sparks, he pulled out a small, blackened object: a small, silver-tipped object that glittered in the firelight. It was a second key, identical to the first. Julian’s mouth dropped open as Marcus Reed pointed a accusing finger. "That’s the key to the vault in the master's bedroom! The boy was trying to burn the evidence of his theft!" Julian could only shake his head, his tears flowing freely now, while Dr. Aris stepped forward, his eyes narrowing as he looked at the blackened metal. Thorne held the key up, his expression unreadable, as he noted that the vault key was surprisingly cool to the touch despite being in the ashes. 
"Wait, there’s only one safe," Thorne said, his voice quiet. "And only one key." 
The room fell into a stunned silence as Thorne held both keys side by side. One was blackened by the fire, the other pristine. Julian looked from the keys to the detective, his eyes wide with a growing realization. Marcus Reed’s face turned a deep shade of crimson as he sputtered, "What does that mean? There must be two keys!"

Thorne moved back to the victim’s body, his gaze settling on the letter opener still protruding from Sterling’s chest. He noticed a small, faint bruise on the man’s neck—a slight, bluish mark that looked more like an injection point than a bruise from a struggle. Marcus Reed, his patience wearing thin, stepped forward to demand an arrest. "The evidence is overwhelming, Thorne! The medical training, the gambling debts, the inheritance change—Julian killed him! Arrest him now!" Julian’s face was a mask of despair, his voice a hoarse croak as he pleaded for his life. Dr. Aris leaned in, his expression unreadable as he studied the mark on the neck, but he remained silent as Thorne’s eyes drifted to the housekeeper’s shaking hands. "Mrs. Miller," Thorne said quietly, his voice cutting through the tension. "You’ve been in service to the Sterling family for many years, haven't you?" Clara’s voice was a mere whisper, her eyes fixed on the empty brandy decanter. "Twenty years, sir. I’ve seen everything." She looked at Julian, her gaze heavy with pity, before turning away to face the cold hearth. Thorne then moved to the desk again, his fingers tracing the black smudge once more, and this time, he noticed something else—a small, dark hair caught in the drawer’s mechanism.

Thorne’s fingers traced the edge of the mahogany desk again, the black grease staining his fingertips. He leaned down and sniffed it, his brow furrowing as he recognized the faint, sharp smell of graphite. Marcus Reed’s eyes narrowed as he watched the detective, his posture tense and his hands still shoved deep into his pockets. "Probably just a loose pen nib, Thorne! We should be calling the constabulary before the boy tries to flee again." Dr. Aris stepped forward, his eyes also fixed on the smudge as he adjusted his medical bag, his movements slow and deliberate. Julian, meanwhile, was still sobbing in the corner, his shoulders shaking with the weight of the accusation. Clara Miller moved toward the tea service on the side table, her hands trembling as she tried to pour a cup of cooling tea for the hysterical boy, her gaze fixed on the empty brandy decanter. Thorne stood up, his gaze sweeping the room before settling on Marcus Reed’s boots, which were slightly damp and caked with the same black graphite from the floor near the desk.

Thorne moved back to the victim’s body, his gaze falling on the heavy, silver-tipped cane that lay abandoned near the desk. He noticed that the top of the cane was slightly bent, as if it had been struck against something hard. Marcus Reed, his face a mask of practiced indifference, stepped forward. "Sterling always had a bad knee, Thorne. He probably tripped and dropped it." Dr. Aris bent down to examine the cane, his clinical eye scanning the metal for any sign of a struggle. "Indeed, the impact mark is consistent with a sudden fall," the doctor observed, his voice calm and detached. Julian Vane, however, looked up from his hands, his eyes widening in recognition. "I saw that cane! It was in the master’s hand when he was... when he was shouting at me!" Clara Miller’s breath hitched, and she looked from the cane to Marcus, who only offered a cold, calculating smile. Thorne took note of the way the doctor’s hand brushed the black smudge on the desk as he stood back up, his expression unreadable.

Thorne reached out his hand and touched the black smudge on the desk again, this time feeling its consistency. It wasn't grease at all, but a thick, viscous ink that was still wet to the touch. He noticed that the ledger’s last page was smeared, a detail he hadn't fully appreciated before. Marcus Reed let out a cynical chuckle, his eyes mocking. "Julian must have been in such a hurry to finish his work that he didn't even wait for the ink to dry before he murdered his uncle." Julian sobbed that he hadn't even touched the ledger, his fingers stained only by the blood on his uncle’s shirt. Dr. Aris stepped forward, his expression curious as he leaned over the desk. "A most unfortunate mess," the doctor observed, his voice calm and detached. Thorne turned back to the others, his eyes catching a small, dark stain on Clara Miller’s white apron, a mark she tried to hide behind her hands as he approached.

Thorne moved toward Clara, his footsteps heavy in the hushed room. She shrank back against the wall as he reached out a hand to her apron. "Mrs. Miller, this stain here... what is it?" Clara’s voice was a mere whisper, her eyes darting between Thorne and Marcus Reed. "It’s... it’s just tea, sir. From when I brought the master his evening tray." Julian let out a small, tired laugh, his voice a hoarse croak as he accused her of lying. Dr. Aris stepped closer, his medical bag clicking as he moved, and peered down through his spectacles. "It’s not tea, Detective. It’s some kind of ink, and quite fresh at that." Marcus Reed’s face darkened, his brow furrowing as he looked from Clara to Julian. "What are you suggesting, doctor? That the housekeeper was helping the boy with his forgery?" Clara’s eyes widened with terror as she stammered a denial, her hands trembling so violently that she nearly dropped the small, silver-tipped matchbox she had been holding. 
Thorne looked at the matchbox and then back at the desk, his eyes narrowing as he realized something he hadn't before. 
"Mrs. Miller, did you see anyone else in the library before you brought the tea?" Clara’s voice was barely a whisper as she shook her head, her gaze fixed on the doctor’s bag. "No, sir. Just the master and Master Julian. And then the door was locked." 
Thorne turned back to the room, his eyes scanning the walls for any sign of another entrance. He noticed a small, nearly invisible seam in the oak paneling, just behind where Marcus Reed was standing. "Mr. Reed, would you mind stepping aside for a moment?" Marcus Reed’s face flushed with anger as he moved, his eyes narrowing. "What is it, Thorne? More of your detective games?" Thorne reached out his hand and pressed a small, hidden latch in the paneling. The wall swung open with a soft, oiled click, revealing a narrow, dark passage that led deep into the manor. 
Julian let out a gasp of surprise, his eyes widening as he looked into the darkness. "I... I didn't know about that!" Marcus Reed’s face paled as he looked into the passage, his eyes darting toward the door as if he were looking for a way out. Dr. Aris stepped forward, his expression curious as he peered into the gloom. "A secret passage," the doctor mused, his voice calm and detached. "It seems we have a more complex mystery than we first thought." 
Clara Miller’s eyes widened with terror as she looked into the passage, her hands trembling so violently that she nearly dropped the silver-tipped matchbox again. 
Thorne reached out his hand and took the matchbox from her, his eyes narrowing as he looked at the silver tip. It was not a matchbox at all, but a small, cleverly disguised inkwell. 
"Mrs. Miller, I believe you have some explaining to do." Clara’s voice was a mere whisper as she looked from Thorne to Marcus Reed, her eyes filled with terror. "I... I didn't mean to, sir. He made me do it!" 
Marcus Reed’s face darkened with anger as he looked at Clara, his eyes narrowing with a predatory gleam. "What are you talking about, woman? I didn't make you do anything!" 
Julian let out a small, tired laugh, his voice a hoarse croak as he looked at Marcus. "You’re the one, Marcus! You’re the one who was trying to frame me for my uncle’s murder!" 
Thorne turned back to the room, his eyes scanning the faces of the four suspects. He noticed that Dr. Aris was watching the exchange with a strange, contemplative expression, his fingers tapping rhythmically on the handle of his medical bag. 
"It seems we have a more complex mystery than we first thought," Thorne repeated, his voice calm and steady. "But I think I’m beginning to see the truth." 
He turned to Julian and looked at him for a long moment. "Mr. Vane, I believe you’re telling the truth. You didn't kill your uncle." 
Julian let out a small, tired sigh of relief, his eyes filled with tears. "Thank you, Detective. Thank you." 
Thorne turned to Marcus Reed and looked at him with a cold, unwavering gaze. "Mr. Reed, I believe you have some explaining to do. About the secret passage, and the ink on Mrs. Miller’s apron." 
Marcus Reed’s face flushed with anger as he looked at Thorne, his eyes narrowing. "What are you talking about, Thorne? I didn't have anything to do with this!" 
Thorne reached out his hand and pointed to the secret passage. "I believe you were the one who used this passage to enter the library and kill Arthur Sterling. And then you used the ink to forge the inheritance change in the ledger." 
Marcus Reed let out a harsh, cynical laugh, his eyes mocking. "You have no proof of that, Thorne. No proof at all." 
Thorne turned to Dr. Aris and looked at him for a long moment. "Dr. Aris, I believe you have something to tell us about the sedative." 
Dr. Aris stepped forward, his expression curious as he looked at Thorne. "What do you mean, Detective?" 
Thorne reached out his hand and took the vial from the doctor's hand. "This vial... it was not prescribed to Julian Vane. It was prescribed to you." 
Dr. Aris’s eyes widened with surprise as he looked at the vial, his face turning a sickly shade of gray. "I... I don't understand, Detective."

"I didn't see you in the kitchen, Clara," he whispered, his voice rising in panic. "I saw you coming out of the library when I arrived! You had that silver tray in your hands!" Clara’s face drained of color, her mouth working silently as she looked at Thorne. 
The detective’s eyes flickered from her to the black smudge on the desk, then to the medical bag, and finally to the large, heavy key Thorne had retrieved from the fire. 
He noted that the silver key was still surprisingly cool to the touch, despite being in the ashes. Thorne’s gaze settled on Marcus Reed, who was now looming over Clara, his voice harsh as he demanded the truth. "What were you doing in the library, Clara? What did you do with the money?" Clara sobbed that she had only been checking on the master, but the way she kept glancing at Marcus Reed spoke volumes. Thorne turned his attention back to the desk, his mind racing through the clues—the black smudge, the silver key, the gambling debt, and the knowledge of anatomy. 
The pieces were starting to fall into place. 
He noticed a small, glinting object on the floor near the medical bag: a needle, half-hidden beneath the rug. 
Thorne stepped over to retrieve it, his eyes catching the doctor’s expression. Dr. Aris’s face was a mask of professional curiosity, yet his hand was tightening on his bag. 
Thorne stood up, the needle held carefully in his gloved fingers. "It seems we have another piece of evidence," he said, his voice echoing in the quiet room. 
Marcus Reed barked a laugh, pointing at Julian. "Another of the boy’s toys, no doubt! He’s the one with the medical training, isn’t he?" 
Julian’s eyes widened, his head shaking frantically. "No! I never used that! I don’t even have any needles!" 
Thorne’s gaze never left Dr. Aris, who merely nodded in clinical interest. "A most intriguing find, Detective. It seems someone was prepared for more than just a murder." 
Clara Miller’s eyes darted toward the door, her hands still clutching her apron as she whispered that she had seen Julian with a similar needle earlier in the day. 
The case against Julian was becoming overwhelming, yet Thorne’s eyes were fixed on the black smudge on the desk. 
He moved to the ledger once more, his fingers tracing the smeared ink. 
The smudge was thick, viscous, and... remarkably similar to the black grease on the door hinges. 
Thorne’s mind raced as he realized the truth. 
The black smudge wasn't ink at all—it was a form of lubricant, used to silence the movement of a heavy door. 
But the door hinges were clean. 
Thorne’s eyes moved to the medical bag, and then to Dr. Aris’s hand. 
The doctor’s hand was covered in the same black grease, barely visible against his dark suit. 
Thorne’s voice was steady as he spoke. "Dr. Aris, could you explain why you have lubricant on your hand?" 
Dr. Aris’s expression didn't change, but his eyes narrowed. "I was just checking the lock on my bag, Detective. It’s been sticking lately." 
Marcus Reed let out a cynical laugh, pointing at Julian. "Don’t waste your time on the doctor, Thorne! The boy’s the one who’s been caught red-handed!" 
Thorne’s gaze never left Dr. Aris. 
"The needle, the lubricant, the knowledge of anatomy... and the inheritance." 
Thorne turned back to the ledger, his fingers tracing the smeared ink. 
"The inheritance wasn't for Julian. It was for Dr. Aris." 
The room went deathly still. 
Julian’s eyes widened, his jaw dropping in shock. 
Marcus Reed’s face turned a deep shade of red, his voice booming. "What? That’s impossible! Arthur would never leave anything to him!" 
Thorne’s voice was calm as he explained. "The ledger was altered. The name 'Julian' was written over 'Aris'. The lubricant was used to silence the door while the doctor committed the crime, and the needle was used to deliver the sedative before the fatal blow." 
Dr. Aris’s face was a mask of cold fury, his eyes burning with a dark light. 
"You have no proof, Detective." 
Thorne reached into his pocket and pulled out the small, silver key. 
"Actually, I do. This key was found in the fire, but it’s cool to the touch. It was placed there after the fire had died down." 
Thorne’s eyes met Dr. Aris’s. 
"And the black smudge on your hand is identical to the one on the desk." 
Dr. Aris’s face twisted into a snarl, his hand reaching for something in his bag. 
"You’ll never prove it!" 
Before he could move, Marcus Reed’s heavy hand landed on his shoulder, pinning him in place. 
"I think he just did," Reed growled, his voice thick with contempt. 
Julian let out a sob of relief, his head falling into his hands. 
Clara Miller stood by the door, her eyes wide with shock. 
The truth had been revealed. 
Dr. Aris was the killer. 
Thorne turned to Julian, his voice gentle. "I’m sorry, Mr. Vane. You were a convenient scapegoat." 
Julian only nodded, his tears flowing freely. 
The storm outside continued to howl, but inside Blackwood Manor, the mystery had finally been solved. 
Thorne walked to the window and looked out at the white expanse of snow. 
The killer had been caught, and the truth had been found. 
The case was closed.

Thorne bent down to retrieve the black silk thread, his eyes narrowing as he compared it to the dark blue jacket of Julian Vane. Thorne turned his attention to Marcus Reed, whose large, heavy boots were stained with the same gray ash that had covered the key. Thorne’s eyes drifted back to the small, white powder he had found beneath the victim’s fingernails, then to the vial of sedative that had been discovered in the armchair. Thorne turned to Dr. Aris, his voice a low, steady rumble. "Tell me, Doctor, why would a man who’s been dead for hours still have fresh ink on his hands?" Dr. Aris paused, his eyes narrowing. Clara Miller let out a small, stifled cry, her hands shaking so violently that she dropped her lamp, which shattered on the floor in a spray of sparks and oil. The room plunged into a terrifying, flickering darkness as the others scrambled for a light. Thorne’s hand flew to his own holster as he called out for everyone to stay still, his voice a command that brooked no argument. Through the gloom, the detective could see the silhouette of a man standing by the desk, his hand reaching for the ledger. It was Marcus Reed, his face a mask of desperation as he tried to grab the book and flee. Thorne stepped forward, his gun drawn and ready. "It’s over, Marcus. The ink on the ledger is still wet because you were the one who forged it, not Julian." Marcus froze, his eyes darting toward the door. "You have no proof!" he spat, his voice a hiss. Marcus’s eyes widened as he looked down at his own sleeve, where a small, ragged tear had been hidden by his large hands. Dr. Aris stepped forward, his voice a low, calm rumble.
